title: Machine learning-enabled wastewater-based surveillance for emerging pathogen detection and monitoring: current applications, challenges, and future prospects

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Machine learning-enabled wastewater-based surveillance for emerging pathogen detection and monitoring: current applications, challenges, and future prospects》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Anomaly and fluctuation detection for early warning · S002-S2002-p1】The task of anomaly and fluctuation detection differs from forecasting. Rather than estimating the future value of a public-health indicator, it identifies unexpected spikes, shifts, or departures from baseline trends that may signal an emerging outbreak [47–50]. The methods used for this purpose span the first two layers defined in the section on data analysis in WBS and can be combined.

【Statistical detection and signal quality · S002-S2002-S3001-p1】At the statistical layer (L1), Ensor et al. applied online trend estimation and deviation detection to sub-sewershed SARS-CoV-2 RNA time series, providing a near-real-time framework for identifying local departures from broader wastewater trends [47]. Because the model is fitted to the series itself, it requires no paired clinical labels and can be updated as each new measurement arrives, allowing it to be incorporated into routine reporting pipelines. Related L1 procedures and quality-control measures address the same problem from the data-quality side: Bayesian smoothing supports short-term projection and outlier identification [48], and routine quality-control indicators, in particular flow rate and gene-segment ratios, help separate measurement outliers from genuine concentration changes across more than 150 treatment plants [49]. Measurements below the limit of quantification require separate treatment, because substituting a fixed value biases both the estimated concentration and its trend. Two censored-data smoothers developed for this purpose – an autoregressive smoother robust to outliers, in operational use by the French national network, and a left-censored dynamic linear model – were compared under cross-validation with each other and with a simple moving average using data from 286 sewage treatment works in England. Both tracked regional case-rate positivity more closely than untransformed data or the moving average; at comparable predictive accuracy, the dynamic linear model was more parsimonious and faster to compute [45,79]. In an early-warning system, distinguishing a measurement artifact from a genuine epidemiological change is part of the detection task.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Machine learning-enabled wastewater-based surveillance for emerging pathogen detection and monitoring: current applications, challenges, and future prospects》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Model selection and feature design · S003-S2002-S3001-p1】Model selection further complicates ML-enabled WBS, because no single model family is consistently optimal across surveillance objectives and data settings. Depending on the task, candidate models span all four layers defined in the section on data analysis in WBS, from correlation and regression models to tree ensembles, recurrent architectures, and semi-mechanistic frameworks. The studies reviewed in the section on predictive modelling and forecasting show that performance depends on both the data available and the model design. Vaughan et al. found that forecast accuracy depended chiefly on sampling frequency and training-set size, with the contribution of catchment population less clear [58]; Dejus et al. found that performance depended on both algorithm choice and the inclusion of variant-related features [53]; and Ai et al. found that models incorporating temporal structure outperformed those fitted without it on the same dataset [52]. Model selection in ML-enabled WBS is therefore not merely a choice among algorithms; it also depends on feature availability, prediction horizon, geographic transferability, interpretability, and the public-health objective. Geographic transferability remains particularly underexamined.

【Laboratory methods for pathogen detection and monitoring in WBS · S001-S2003-p1】Pathogen detection and quantification form the analytical foundation of WBS. Traditional surveillance approaches primarily rely on targeted molecular assays such as quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) and digital PCR (dPCR), which enable sensitive detection and quantification of known pathogens in wastewater samples [39,40,72]. These technologies underpin most of the detections summarized in Table 1 and remain the backbone of routine WBS programmes [3].

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Machine learning-enabled wastewater-based surveillance for emerging pathogen detection and monitoring: current applications, challenges, and future prospects》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Performance limits and context dependence · S002-S2001-S3003-p1】Reported performance has also been inconsistent. Vaughan et al. evaluated random-forest time-series forecasting (L2) across 108 sites in five regions and found accuracy to depend chiefly on sampling frequency and training-set size, with the contribution of catchment population less clear [58]. In a semi-mechanistic Bayesian forecasting model (L4) for state-level hospital admissions, adding wastewater data left overall performance essentially unchanged, although it improved or degraded forecasts substantially at particular locations and dates [59]. Model complexity is therefore not a benefit in itself: predictive performance depends on sampling frequency, training-set size, location, and forecasting context, and adding wastewater data does not improve forecasts uniformly.

【Validation under temporal and spatial dependence · S003-S2002-S3003-p1】Whether such transfer failures are detected depends on how models are validated, and WBS data pose a structural difficulty. Wastewater concentration series and the epidemic curves they track are both strongly autocorrelated: consecutive observations are statistically dependent and often highly similar rather than independent draws, so a randomly partitioned series can place temporally adjacent observations in both the training and test sets, and the resulting error estimate may partly reflect interpolation between nearby observations and can overstate genuine forecasting performance. A related problem arises across space, since neighbouring catchments share climate, mobility patterns, and often laboratory methods. Empirical evidence on how far this inflates reported accuracy is mixed: in a comparison of six model-selection procedures on synthetic and real-world series, no systematic under- or overestimation of error was attributable to the dependencies themselves, although blocked cross-validation yielded more robust error estimates than reserving the final segment of each series [104]. In ecological modelling, where spatial and phylogenetic dependence is pervasive, blocked designs have been shown to be preferable to random partitioning wherever the goal is prediction to new data or new predictor space, with the caveat that blocking can itself induce extrapolation by restricting the predictor combinations available for training [105]. Neither literature source is specific to WBS, but both indicate that the partitioning scheme should follow the dependence structure of the data rather than convenience.

sections.title: 图表阅读
sections.text:
《Machine learning-enabled wastewater-based surveillance for emerging pathogen detection and monitoring: current applications, challenges, and future prospects》：图表的原始标题与说明。

【Figure 1. · F0001】Figure 1. Workflow of machine learning-enabled wastewater surveillance. The framework comprises six interconnected stages (1) sampling of wastewater from diverse sources using appropriate strategies; (2) laboratory analysis including sample processing and pathogen detection; (3) data management and harmonization of multi-source heterogeneous data; (4) machine learning analytics for predictive modelling, anomaly detection, and pattern discovery; (5) generation of outputs, visualization, and communication; and (6) translation of insights into public health actions. Abbreviations: qPCR, quantitative polymerase chain reaction; dPCR, digital PCR; ELISA, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay; AMR, antimicrobial resistance; ML, machine learning.

【Figure 2. · F0002】Figure 2. Multimodal data integration and translation to public-health decision support in machine learning-enabled wastewater-based surveillance (WBS). Multiple wastewater, epidemiological, clinical, environmental, sewer-system, population, and contextual data streams are integrated and harmonized before analysis using statistical and machine-learning approaches. Analytical outputs are transformed into surveillance indicators, including early-warning alerts, trend estimates, forecasting results, and variant/AMR profiles, which support public-health interpretation, risk assessment, resource allocation, targeted interventions, and policy decision-making. Continuous feedback enables data reprocessing and model updating.

【Figure 3. · F0003】Figure 3. Challenges and future directions of machine learning in wastewater-based surveillance (WBS). Major challenges for machine learning-enabled WBS include limitations in data quality and availability, methodological complexities in model development and interpretation, and barriers to real-world implementation, scalability, and governance. Future directions focus on standardized data frameworks, multimodal data integration, digital-twin-based mechanistic modelling, explainable and trustworthy analytics, and expansion of WBS applications beyond pathogen surveillance to broader population-health monitoring. Arrows indicate the interrelationships between current challenges and potential future solutions.

sections.title: 复现线索
sections.text:
《Machine learning-enabled wastewater-based surveillance for emerging pathogen detection and monitoring: current applications, challenges, and future prospects》：复现时可直接核对的数据、软件或实现线索。

【Data quality and availability · S003-S2001-p1】High-quality input data are essential for building robust ML models, yet WBS data present several upstream data-quality challenges. These uncertainties propagate into ML models, reducing prediction accuracy, model transferability, and the reliability of downstream public-health interpretation. They do not propagate uniformly: the same data limitation can be minor for one model family and severely distorting for another, so the consequences of data-quality problems should be considered in relation to the model family being used.

【Structural limitations in data availability · S003-S2001-S3003-p1】Limited data availability is a further constraint, and it arises in two distinct ways: the population of interest may not contribute to the sewer, or the target may not be circulating at detectable concentrations. Van den Berg et al. assessed ten child daycare centres in the Netherlands for wastewater surveillance and found none suitable, because the centres were embedded in mixed-use or multi-tenant buildings and installing dedicated sampling points was judged disproportionately demanding in resources and permissions [100]. The same study notes a second and separate limitation, that diaper-wearing children do not use sanitary facilities and therefore do not contribute directly to the wastewater stream, so that even a feasible sampling point would under-represent the population of interest. The second constraint appears when the target itself is scarce: Casado-Martín et al. monitored SARS-CoV-2, influenza A and B, and RSV-A and RSV-B in a mid-sized Spanish city over twelve months and found that SARS-CoV-2 concentrations correlated with reported cases (r > 0.5), whereas influenza A and B were not detected, RSV-B was detected in only two samples, and RSV-A circulation declined under non-pharmaceutical interventions [101]. Data availability in WBS is therefore both pathogen- and population-dependent, and a run of non-detects may reflect under-representation of the population of interest, an unsuitable sampling point, or genuinely absent circulation – distinctions that a concentration time series alone cannot resolve.
